summary: Jesus comes down from the mountain and authority becomes action. He touches a man with a skin disease, praises a Gentile centurion's trust, heals Peter's mother-in-law and a crowd, then crosses the lake after warning would-be followers about cost. A storm exposes the disciples as ‘little-faith,’ and across the water demons recognize the Son of God before the townspeople ask him to leave.
whyItMatters: The chapter tests whether the teacher's authority reaches bodies, distance, creation, hostile spirits, and outsiders. Matthew also refuses triumphalism: healing authority travels with homelessness, costly following, frightened disciples, and rejection.

context.author: Anonymous narrator grouping miracle traditions after the Sermon
context.audience: Readers learning how word, authority, faith, and fulfillment connect
context.date: Late-first-century composition using material also found in Mark and Luke
context.setting: Galilee, Capernaum, the lake, and Gentile-associated territory across it
context.literaryForm: Three miracle clusters interrupted by discipleship sayings

outline.heading: Cleansing by touch and healing by a word
Household and crowd restored; Isaiah fulfilled
The cost of crossing with Jesus
Storm, little faith, and authority over demons

keyVerses.text: The centurion answered, “Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
keyVerses.why: The officer interprets Jesus's authority through command effective at a distance.

keyVerses.text: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.”
keyVerses.why: Matthew reads the healings through Isaiah's servant language of bearing weakness.

keyVerses.text: The men marveled, saying, “What kind of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
keyVerses.why: The disciples' question carries the reader from admired teacher toward a larger identity claim.

questions.question: What does ‘leprosy’ mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The biblical term covers a range of serious skin conditions and is not a precise diagnosis of modern Hansen's disease. The central social word is ‘clean’: the man seeks restoration to communal and worship life. Jesus touches him before the condition changes, crossing the isolation without becoming a source of uncleanness.

questions.question: Why send the healed man to a priest?
questions.answer: Levitical procedure gave priests responsibility to inspect and certify cleansing. Jesus's command restores the man publicly and supplies testimony within Israel's legal framework. ‘Show yourself’ means bodily healing is not complete while exclusion remains unaddressed.

questions.question: How does the centurion understand ‘authority’?
questions.answer: Exousia is delegated right and effective command. As an officer under authority who commands others, he reasons that Jesus need not be physically present: ‘say only a word.’ Matthew uses a Gentile military figure to recognize how Jesus's authority works while also showing unusual humility about entering a Jewish home.

questions.question: Does ‘he took our infirmities’ mean Jesus can never allow sickness?
questions.answer: Matthew quotes Isaiah 53 to interpret a concentrated healing ministry as Jesus bearing human weakness. The verb ‘took’ is not a formula for blaming an unhealed person or denying later suffering; the same Gospel will portray sickness, persecution, and death among faithful people. The citation identifies compassionate vocation, not a guarantee on demand.

questions.question: Is ‘let the dead bury their own dead’ a rejection of family duty?
questions.answer: The sentence is deliberate prophetic shock. Burial was a weighty obligation, and the saying makes the kingdom's claim sound immediate and absolute. It may concern a request to remain home until a living father eventually dies, but the text does not say. Either way, Jesus refuses a discipleship postponed indefinitely by socially compelling reasons.

questions.question: Why call the disciples ‘you of little faith’ during a lethal storm?
questions.answer: Oligopistoi is Matthew's recurring label for followers whose trust proves too small under pressure. It is not ‘no faith’: they enter the boat and call Jesus Lord, yet fear interprets reality more powerfully than his presence. The repeated term links this storm to anxiety, Peter sinking, and the bread misunderstanding.

questions.question: Why do the demons ask whether Jesus has come ‘before the time’?
questions.answer: They recognize both identity and an appointed future judgment that human characters have not yet articulated. Matthew's language holds an ‘already/not yet’ tension: God's rule is acting now, while final defeat remains associated with a coming time. Recognition from demons is not discipleship; they know and resist.

glossary.def: Ritual and communal status permitting ordinary participation, not merely physical hygiene.
A Roman military officer associated with command of roughly a hundred soldiers, though actual units varied.
